questions.title: A joint at the end of a movable long bone with a joint cavity is which type?
questions.question: A joint found at the end of movable long bones, and containing a joint cavity, would be classified as a:

explanations.A: Correct. A synovial joint is freely mobile, present mostly in the limbs, and is defined by seven named components built around a joint cavity — a fibrous capsule, a synovial membrane lining it, synovial fluid, articular (hyaline) cartilage over the bone ends, ligaments, ligamentous reinforcements and, in some joints, intra-articular structures such as a disc or meniscus. That joint cavity is the feature this stem is pointing at: it is present only in synovial joints, which is exactly why a joint 'at the end of movable long bones, containing a joint cavity' can only be a synovial joint. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints have no such cavity — their bones are held directly together by connective tissue or cartilage — so the cavity itself is the single most reliable feature separating synovial joints from the other two classes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 'Epithelial joint' is not a recognised joint classification; epithelium lines body surfaces and cavities generally, not the articulating surfaces of bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 'Articular joint' is not a distinct class of joint — articular surfaces exist at synovial joints, but the class defined by a joint cavity is named synovial, not articular.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fibrous joint unites bones directly by fibrous tissue and has no joint cavity, the opposite of what this stem describes.

questions.title: The joints between the bones of the skull are called:
questions.question: The joints between the bones of the skull are called:

explanations.A: Correct. A fibrous joint unites bone surfaces by fibrous tissue and is fixed or immobile, and it comes in three named types: syndesmosis (bones held by an interosseous ligament, as at the inferior tibiofibular joint), gomphosis (a tooth root held in its socket by the periodontal ligament), and suture (skull bones held by a thin sutural ligament, which obliterates in old age). The joints between the flat bones of the skull vault are the type example of a suture — the ligament, not just the site, is what earns the name, which is why the department book pairs each fibrous-joint type with its own named connective tissue. As a fibrous joint, a suture permits essentially no movement, consistent with the skull's own job of protecting the brain rather than moving around it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint unites bones by fibrocartilage in the midline (for example the pubic symphysis or an intervertebral disc), not the skull bones, which are united by fibrous tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A hinge joint is a synovial joint with a cavity, permitting flexion and extension (for example the elbow); the immobile skull bones share neither its cavity nor its movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synovial joint has a joint cavity and is freely mobile; the skull bones are united directly by fibrous tissue with no cavity and essentially no movement.

questions.title: Which is the only temporary joint?
questions.question: The only temporary joint, among the following, is:

explanations.C: Correct. A primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) unites bones by hyaline cartilage, is usually temporary, and ossifies as growth finishes — the epiphyseal (growth) plate is its type example, and once it ossifies the two bone ends it joined become one continuous bone. A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), by contrast, unites bones by fibrocartilage in the midline and is permanent for life, as at the pubic symphysis or an intervertebral disc — so 'temporary' is exactly the property that tells the two cartilaginous joint types apart. Gomphosis (a fibrous joint) and plane synovial joints are both permanent structures with no such ossifying end-point, which is why neither is a candidate for 'the only temporary joint' in this list.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Gomphosis is a fibrous joint (a tooth root held in its socket by the periodontal ligament) and is permanent, not temporary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint is permanent — the opposite of the primary cartilaginous joint's temporary, ossifying nature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A plane synovial joint is a permanent, freely mobile joint with a cavity; it does not ossify away with age.

questions.title: Which is NOT a character of the synovial joint?
questions.question: The synovial joint has the following characters, EXCEPT:

options.A: Allows a considerable range of movement
options.B: Their articular surfaces are covered by elastic cartilage
options.D: Minimal synovial fluid within its cavity

explanations.B: Correct. The articular surfaces of a synovial joint are covered by hyaline cartilage, not elastic cartilage — smooth, avascular and lubricated by synovial fluid, which nourishes it in the absence of a direct blood supply. Elastic cartilage is a different histological type entirely, found where a structure needs to bend and spring back (the auricle of the ear, the epiglottis), not where it needs a slick, load-bearing joint surface. The other three statements are all genuine synovial-joint properties — a considerable range of movement, a surrounding fibrous capsule, and a joint cavity that normally holds only a thin (minimal) film of fluid rather than a large pooled volume — which is exactly why the false one has to be spotted among three true statements.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A considerable range of movement is a genuine character of synovial joints, not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Being covered by a fibrous capsule is a genuine character of synovial joints, not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The joint cavity of a synovial joint is potential, holding only a thin, minimal film of fluid under normal conditions; this is a genuine character, not the exception.

questions.title: The intervertebral disc is an example of which joint type?
questions.question: The intervertebral disc articulates the bodies of adjacent vertebrae. It is an example of a:

explanations.B: Correct. A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) unites bones by fibrocartilage, sits in the midline, is permanent, and permits slight movement — and the intervertebral disc, uniting the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae, is the department book's own worked example of exactly this joint type, alongside the pubic symphysis. Its fibrocartilaginous structure (an outer anulus fibrosus around an inner nucleus pulposus) is what allows the slight give between vertebrae that a primary cartilaginous joint, being temporary and effectively rigid until it ossifies, could not provide. Distinguishing the two cartilaginous joint types by permanence and the amount of movement they allow is exactly what this item and the 'only temporary joint' item elsewhere in this bank are both testing, from opposite directions.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A primary cartilaginous joint is temporary and ossifies with growth (the epiphyseal plate is its type example); the intervertebral disc is permanent, not temporary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A fibrous joint unites bone directly by fibrous tissue with no cartilage; the intervertebral disc is a cartilaginous structure, not a fibrous one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A hinge synovial joint has a joint cavity and permits flexion/extension around one axis; the intervertebral disc has no cavity and is a cartilaginous, not synovial, joint.

questions.title: Which joint type is the most fixed, with no potential for movement?
questions.question: The most fixed type of joint, which does not allow any range of movement and has no potential ever to do so, is:

explanations.B: Correct. Of the two cartilaginous joint types, only the primary cartilaginous joint permits no movement at all by definition — its hyaline cartilage forms a rigid, temporary union (the epiphyseal plate) that ossifies away rather than ever loosening, so there is no 'potential' for movement to develop the way there is at a secondary cartilaginous joint (which permits slight movement) or even a fibrous joint. This is the department bank's own convention for ranking fixity, and it turns on the word 'potential': a suture or a syndesmosis is also very restricted in movement, but neither is defined as permitting literally none, and both remain living fibrous unions rather than the rigid cartilage-to-bone conversion a primary cartilaginous joint undergoes. Reading this item alongside 'the only temporary joint' elsewhere in the bank makes the intended logic clear — both point at the same primary-cartilaginous-joint fact from different angles: complete fixity, and eventual ossification, are two sides of the same property.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint held by an interosseous ligament (as at the inferior tibiofibular joint); it is very restricted but is a fibrous union, not the joint type the bank's own key names as most fixed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A secondary cartilaginous joint permits slight movement by definition (as at an intervertebral disc), which is the opposite of allowing no movement at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sutures are fibrous joints holding the skull bones together; they are very restricted but are not the bank's own answer for the joint type with no potential ever to move.

questions.title: Which synovial joint type allows the fullest range of movement, including circumduction?
questions.question: Which of the following types of synovial joint allows adduction, abduction, flexion, extension, medial and lateral rotation, and circumduction?

explanations.C: Correct. The movements possible at a synovial joint follow directly from how many axes its shape allows it to move around, and a ball-and-socket joint is triaxial — its spherical head sitting in a matching socket lets it move around three perpendicular axes at once, giving adduction, abduction, flexion, extension, and medial and lateral rotation, and circumduction as the smooth combination of all of them. A hinge joint, by contrast, is uniaxial and permits only flexion and extension; a pivot joint is also uniaxial but for rotation alone (as at the radio-ulnar joints); and a plane joint permits only small gliding movements with no fixed axis at all. Naming the joint type from its full list of possible movements — rather than from a single movement in isolation — is exactly the skill this item and the department's other joint-classification items are built to test.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A pivot joint is uniaxial and permits rotation only (as at the superior and inferior radio-ulnar joints), not the full list of movements this stem describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hinge joint is uniaxial and permits flexion and extension only, never abduction, adduction or rotation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A plane joint permits only small gliding movements between flat articular surfaces, with no single fixed axis and no rotation or circumduction.

questions.title: Pneumatic bones are called so because they contain:
questions.question: The pneumatic bones are called so because they contain:

explanations.D: Correct. By shape, bone falls into six classes, and a pneumatic bone is the class defined by containing air-filled cavities — chiefly the skull bones grouped around the nose (the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary sinuses). The name 'pneumatic' comes directly from this feature, exactly the way 'flat' names bones built as two compact plates around a spongy layer, and 'sesamoid' names a bone embedded in a tendon: each of the six shape classes is named for the structural feature that puts a bone in it. Bone marrow content, lymphatic richness and cell density are not what defines any of the six shape classes, which is why none of them is the reason a pneumatic bone carries that name.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Bone marrow content is not what defines the pneumatic bone class; air-filled cavities are.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphatic richness is not what defines the pneumatic bone class; air-filled cavities are.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Numerous bone cells describe cellularity, not the structural feature — air cavities — that gives the pneumatic bone class its name.

questions.title: The bones of the skull cap are classified as examples of which bone shape?
questions.question: The bones of the skull cap are classified as examples of:

explanations.A: Correct. A flat bone is two thin plates of compact bone with a spongy layer between them, and the skull cap (vault) is the department book's own worked example, alongside the scapula and the ribs — in the skull specifically, the two plates are called the outer and inner tables and the spongy layer between them the diploe. This sandwich structure is exactly what gives the skull vault both some lightness (from the spongy diploe) and mechanical protection (from the two compact outer plates), which is the structural reason flat bones are used to enclose the brain rather than, say, long bones. Short bones (the carpals and tarsals), long bones (with a shaft and two expanded ends) and irregular bones (such as a vertebra) each have a visibly different structure from this two-plates-and-diploe pattern, which is why the skull cap sorts unambiguously into the flat-bone class.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Short bones are spongy bone under a thin compact shell (the carpal and tarsal bones); the skull cap's two-plate, diploe structure does not match this.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Long bones have two expanded ends and a shaft; the skull cap is a curved plate, not a shaft-and-ends structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Irregular bones (such as a vertebra) have an irregular shape with projecting processes and are built like a short bone; the skull cap's flat, two-plate structure does not match this.

questions.title: The function of pneumatic bones is all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.question: The function of pneumatic bones is all of the following, EXCEPT:

options.A: To decrease the weight of the skull
options.C: To provide resonance of the voice
options.D: To regulate the temperature around the brain

explanations.B: Correct. The air cavities of a pneumatic bone do three genuine jobs — lightening the skull, giving the voice resonance, and warming (and, closely related, helping regulate the temperature of) inspired air on its way past the brain — but nourishing the adjacent structures is not one of them. Nourishment of nearby tissue is the job of a blood supply, not an air-filled cavity; an air space carries no vessels of its own and so cannot deliver nutrients to anything around it. This is a variant of the same pneumatic-bone-function fact tested elsewhere in this bank with a different, mechanical-strength distractor, showing the same true three functions paired against two different false ones across the department's own item bank.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Decreasing the weight of the skull is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Providing resonance of the voice is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Regulating (warming) the temperature of air around the brain is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.

questions.title: The arm is described as ___ to the forearm.
questions.question: The arm is ........... to the forearm.

explanations.A: Correct. Proximal and distal measure distance from the root of a limb — proximal nearer the trunk, distal further from it — and the arm (the segment between shoulder and elbow) sits nearer the limb's root than the forearm does, so the arm is proximal to the forearm. Medial and lateral instead measure distance from the median plane, a different reference point entirely, which is why they cannot correctly describe how the arm relates to the forearm along the limb's own long axis. Keeping the reference point straight — the limb's own root for proximal/distal, the median plane for medial/lateral — is exactly the distinction this item and the terms-of-position items elsewhere in the department bank are built to test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Distal means further from the limb's root; the arm is nearer the root than the forearm, so 'distal' has the relationship backwards.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Medial measures distance from the median plane, not from a limb's root, so it does not correctly describe the arm's relationship to the forearm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lateral measures distance from the median plane, not from a limb's root, so it does not correctly describe the arm's relationship to the forearm.

questions.title: Which plane divides the body into two (right and left) halves?
questions.question: The plane which divides the body into two halves is called the ........... plane.

explanations.B: Correct. Each of the three cardinal anatomical planes is named by the two parts it leaves behind, and the sagittal (median) plane runs vertically front-to-back through the midline, leaving equal right and left halves of the body behind — the one plane, of the three, that produces two genuinely equal halves rather than an upper/lower or front/back split. The coronal (frontal) plane instead leaves a front (anterior) and a back (posterior) part, and the transverse (horizontal) plane leaves an upper (superior) and a lower (inferior) part; 'longitudinal' is not one of the three named cardinal planes at all. Naming a plane from the pair of parts it produces, rather than from its orientation in isolation, is exactly the logic this item and the transverse-plane item elsewhere in this bank are both built to test.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronal (frontal) plane divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts, not into two halves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The transverse (horizontal) plane divides the body into upper and lower parts, not into two halves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Longitudinal' is not one of the three named cardinal anatomical planes.

questions.title: The xiphisternal junction is considered which type of joint?
questions.question: The xiphisternal junction is considered as a:

explanations.C: Correct. The xiphisternal junction, where the xiphoid process meets the body of the sternum, is another worked example of a secondary cartilaginous joint — permanent, midline, and united by fibrocartilage rather than by a joint cavity or by hyaline cartilage. The same joint type is illustrated elsewhere in this bank by the intervertebral disc and, classically, by the pubic symphysis; all three share the defining combination of a midline site, fibrocartilage, permanence, and a small amount of give rather than free movement. Recognising the same joint type across several different named sites — the sternum, the vertebral column, the pelvis — is exactly the transfer this item is testing, rather than memorising the xiphisternal junction as an isolated fact.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A fibrous joint unites bone directly by fibrous tissue with no cartilage; the xiphisternal junction is a cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A primary cartilaginous joint is temporary and ossifies with growth; the xiphisternal junction is permanent, matching the secondary, not primary, type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synovial joint has a joint cavity and is freely mobile; the xiphisternal junction has neither a cavity nor free mobility.

questions.title: The main muscle that produces a certain movement is called the:
questions.question: The main muscle that produces a certain movement is called ..............

explanations.C: Correct. A purposeful movement needs four kinds of muscle acting together, each named for what it does to the movement rather than for where it lies, and the prime mover (also called the agonist) is the one that directly initiates and maintains the movement in question — the muscle whose contraction is the movement's main cause. The other three roles support that same movement without producing it themselves: a fixator stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover has something stable to pull against, a synergist cancels an unwanted side-effect the prime mover would otherwise cause at another joint it crosses, and an antagonist relaxes in a controlled way to permit the movement. Naming the prime mover specifically, as the one role defined by actually producing the movement, is exactly what this definitional item is testing before the department bank goes on to test it through the elbow-extension worked example elsewhere.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A fixator stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover can act; it does not itself produce the movement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A synergist prevents an unwanted action at an intermediate joint the prime mover crosses; it does not itself produce the movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Prime mover' is exactly the term for the main muscle producing a movement, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.title: A synovial membrane does which of the following?
questions.question: A synovial membrane ..................

explanations.D: Correct. The synovial membrane is one of the seven named components of a synovial joint: thin, moist and glistening, it covers everything inside the joint capsule except the articular surfaces themselves, and it both secretes and absorbs synovial fluid — the pale, viscous fluid that lubricates the joint and nourishes the avascular articular cartilage. Because it lines the inside of the capsule around the joint cavity, secretes the fluid that fills that cavity, and thereby lubricates the joint, all three listed statements describe the same membrane doing three connected jobs rather than three separate structures. This 'all of the above' item is a useful check that a student can hold all three of the membrane's roles in mind at once, rather than mistaking any one of them for the membrane's only function.
explanations.A: Incorrect on its own, though true — surrounding the joint cavity is only one of the synovial membrane's roles, not the complete answer this item asks for.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own, though true — secreting synovial fluid is only one of the synovial membrane's roles, not the complete answer this item asks for.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own, though true — lubricating the joint is only one of the synovial membrane's roles, not the complete answer this item asks for.

questions.title: The circular movement combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction is called:
questions.question: The circular movement is called ..........

explanations.D: Correct. The movements possible at a joint follow from its type and how many axes it has, and circumduction is the smooth, circular movement produced when flexion, extension, abduction and adduction are combined in sequence rather than performed as separate, isolated movements — it is possible only at joints with at least two axes (an ellipsoid joint such as the wrist) and is most complete at a triaxial ball-and-socket joint. Abduction, adduction and flexion are each just one of the four component movements that, combined, make up circumduction, not the combined movement itself, which is exactly the distinction this definitional item is testing. Naming the compound movement correctly, rather than one of its ingredients, is a common early stumbling block the department bank checks for directly.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Abduction is one of the four component movements combined in circumduction, not the name of the combined circular movement itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adduction is one of the four component movements combined in circumduction, not the name of the combined circular movement itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flexion is one of the four component movements combined in circumduction, not the name of the combined circular movement itself.

questions.title: Which of the following is an example of a pivot joint?
questions.question: The example for a pivot joint is ...............

explanations.C: Correct. Each joint of the upper limb is classified by the shape of its articular surfaces, and the superior (and inferior) radio-ulnar joints are the department's own worked example of a pivot joint: uniaxial, permitting rotation of the radius around the ulna, which is what produces pronation and supination of the forearm. No two neighbouring joints of the upper limb share a type — the elbow beside it is a hinge, and the shoulder further up the same limb is a ball-and-socket joint — which is exactly the pattern this item and the elbow-is-a-hinge item elsewhere in this bank are both testing, one classification at a time.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The elbow joint is a hinge joint (uniaxial, flexion/extension only), not a pivot joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inter-osseous membrane is a fibrous (syndesmosis) union between the shafts of the radius and ulna, not a synovial pivot joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The shoulder joint is a ball-and-socket joint (triaxial), not a pivot joint.

questions.title: The typical movement of the hinge joint includes:
questions.question: The typical movement of the hinge joint includes:

explanations.A: Correct. A hinge joint — the elbow, the interphalangeal joints — is uniaxial and permits flexion and extension only, never abduction, adduction or rotation, so both flexion and extension (the printed key names both, as 'both a & b') are the movements it typically performs. This one-axis restriction is what separates a hinge joint from joints with more axes: an ellipsoid joint such as the wrist adds abduction and adduction to the same flexion/extension pair, and a ball-and-socket joint adds rotation on top of both, but a hinge joint is limited to the single flexion-extension axis by the shape of its own articular surfaces. Recognising which movements a joint's own shape forbids, not only which it allows, is exactly what this item and the pivot-joint-example item elsewhere in this bank are both testing.
explanations.B: Correct alongside A — extension is the hinge joint's other typical movement, paired with flexion around its single axis; the printed key names both together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adduction is a movement of joints with at least two axes (such as an ellipsoid joint); a hinge joint's single axis does not permit it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Medial rotation is a movement of a triaxial joint (such as a ball-and-socket joint); a hinge joint's single axis does not permit rotation at all.

questions.title: Which of the following is a voluntary muscle?
questions.question: Which of the following is a voluntary muscle?

explanations.C: Correct. The three muscle types are told apart by four things at once — site, voluntary control, striation, and nerve supply — and skeletal muscle is the type attached to the skeleton, striated, supplied by somatic nerves, and, uniquely among the three, under voluntary (conscious) control. Cardiac muscle, confined to the myocardium, and smooth muscle, found in the walls of blood vessels and viscera, are both involuntary and supplied by autonomic rather than somatic nerves, which is exactly the feature that rules both of them out here. Voluntary control is the single feature that most directly separates skeletal muscle from the other two types, which is why it is tested as its own item alongside the broader three-way classification elsewhere in the department bank.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle is involuntary, supplied by autonomic nerves, not voluntary skeletal control.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Smooth muscle is involuntary, supplied by autonomic nerves, not voluntary skeletal control.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle is exactly the voluntary muscle type, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.title: Smooth muscle is present in all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.question: The smooth muscle is present in all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.C: Correct. Smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow viscera and blood vessels — the gastrointestinal tract, the urinary bladder, and the walls of blood vessels are all genuine sites — but the myocardium, the muscular wall of the heart, is built of cardiac muscle instead, a separate type that is striated (though less regularly than skeletal muscle) and has its own distinct site, structure and nerve supply. The three muscle types are classified by site among other features precisely so that a structure's own wall tells you its muscle type without ambiguity, and the heart wall's site — the myocardium specifically — is what makes cardiac, not smooth, the correct type there. Confusing cardiac and smooth muscle is an easy mistake because both are involuntary and both are supplied by autonomic nerves, which is exactly why this item isolates site as the deciding feature.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The gastrointestinal tract wall is a genuine site of smooth muscle, not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The urinary bladder wall is a genuine site of smooth muscle, not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood vessel walls are a genuine site of smooth muscle, not the exception.
